newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call money rates at low, guilder weaker.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call money rates at low, guilder weaker.

text.p: Dutch call money fell further on Tuesday as the market was flooded by liquidity before Friday's new three-month credit quota setting, which sets a limit for commercial banks to obtain funds.
Dealers said the market would remain hectic until Friday and rates were likely to fluctuate.
"Other short-dated rates were also pushed lower, along with the sinking call rate," dealers said.
The Dutch guilder became less attractive for investors as money market rates moved down. The guilder was at 112.29 per 100 marks from 112.255 on Monday.
Call money rates, dipping as low as 1.75 percent bid from 2.00 percent on Monday and 2.88 percent on Friday, usually slip before the new credit quota setting, dealers said.
"The rate for call (money) is very low, but there is still quite some business around," said one dealer.

"Banks, which have been saving under the current credit quota, are still willing to offer liquidity at the current low level," said one dealer. "Some return, however little, is better than nothing," he said.
The quota sets an average limit on the amount banks can borrow from the Nederlandsche Bank at the secured loans rate.
The secured loans rate has been at 2.00 percent since April 1996.
Dealers expected call money to rise above the special advances rate of 2.50 percent after Friday.
Special advances are an additional loan offered to commercial banks.
One-month deposits shed two basis points to 2.84 percent bid.
